name: Ashkenaz
title: Son of Gomer and ancestor of a northern people
summary: Ashkenaz was a son of Gomer and a grandson of Japheth, one of Noah's sons. He is mentioned in the Bible's genealogies as an ancestor of a people traditionally associated with the regions around the Black Sea, the Caucasus, and Armenia. The name has been linked to Scythian ethnic groups known from Assyrian sources. In Jewish tradition, the name Ashkenaz was later used for the Germanic lands and gave rise to the term 'Ashkenazi Jews'. In Jeremiah's prophecy against Babylon, the kingdom of Ashkenaz is mentioned together with Ararat and Minni as nations that will be mobilized in God's judgment on the great power.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Noah's genealogy
keyEvents.description: Ashkenaz is listed as a son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth in the post-flood genealogy, which describes the origins of the nations.

keyEvents.title: Repeated in the genealogies of Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Ashkenaz is mentioned again in 1 Chronicles as one of Gomer's sons, in a repetition of the table of nations.

keyEvents.title: The spread of the nations after Babel
keyEvents.description: As a descendant of Japheth, Ashkenaz and his descendants became part of the nations that scattered across the earth after the confusion at the Tower of Babel.

keyEvents.title: The kingdom of Ashkenaz mentioned in Jeremiah's prophecy against Babylon
keyEvents.description: The prophet Jeremiah mentions the kingdom of Ashkenaz together with Ararat and Minni as nations to be mobilized against Babylon in God's judgment.

versions.title: Son of Gomer and descendant of Japheth
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'patriarch' may give the impression that Ashkenaz was one of the great patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob). A more precise title would be 'ancestor' or 'father of a people', since he is primarily known as an ancestor in the table of nations.; [minor] The phrasing "In the book of the prophet Jeremiah" could be simplified slightly for better flow. Otherwise, the summary is good but could be expanded with a brief note on the etymological connection to the term 'Ashkenazi' in Jewish tradition.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a profile like Ashkenaz, it is highly relevant to include notes on the Jewish tradition where 'Ashkenaz' was used for Germany and Northern Europe (and thus the origin of the term 'Ashkenazi Jews'), as well as archaeological/historical connections to peoples in the Anatolia/Black Sea region, possibly the Scythians.

footnotes.text: The name Ashkenaz has been linked to the Assyrian 'Aškuza' and the Greek 'Skythoi' (Scythians), a nomadic people known from areas north of the Black Sea. Assyrian source texts from the 600s BC mention the Aškuza people in connection with conflicts in the region around Armenia and Asia Minor.

In medieval Jewish tradition, the name Ashkenaz was used as a designation for Germany and the Germanic lands. This identification gave rise to the term 'Ashkenazi Jews', referring to Jews of Central and Eastern European origin. The link between biblical Ashkenaz and Germania is already found in early rabbinic literature.

The Hebrew name אַשְׁכְּנַז (ʾAškenaz) has an uncertain etymology. Some scholars have suggested a connection with the Indo-European word for 'Scythians', while others link it to geographical names in ancient Asia Minor. The variation 'Ashkenaz'/'Askenaz' reflects different traditions in the transmission of the text.

In Jeremiah 51:27, the kingdom of Ashkenaz is mentioned together with Ararat (Urartu) and Minni (Mannea)—all known kingdoms in the Armenian highlands and northwest Iran during the 600s BC. This association fits a location of the Ashkenaz people in the region south of the Caucasus.
